source.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinations in Neural Machine Translation
source.authors: Vikas Raunak; Arul Menezes; Marcin Junczys-Dowmunt

record.tranche_reason: Extends the study of memorization and generalization to neural machine translation, measuring perturbation hallucinations for memorized versus random samples and natural hallucinations under added corpus noise.
record.gate_note: The study tests links between memorization, perturbation hallucinations and corpus noise, but does not test the listed claim versions. Its test-BLEU results are for models trained with artificial corpus noise, not the natural-label versus random-label generalization comparison in the claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures translation hallucinations, attention statistics and performance under added corpus noise. It adapts Feldman and Zhang's memorization estimator but does not test their memorized-example removal result (V8). Nor does it test V1–V7. Memorizing deliberately repeated invalid translations while retaining test BLEU is not V1's natural-label versus fixed-random-label comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' main conclusion: memorized samples are more susceptible to perturbation hallucinations, specific corpus-noise patterns generate distinct hallucination patterns, and generated KD/BT data can amplify these patterns. Qualification: the approximate estimator misses many oscillatory hallucinations, BT lacks a clean-model comparator, and the authors' statement that RR yields the fewest hallucinations in both processes contradicts Tables 7–8.
record.recipe_differences: Sequence-to-sequence machine translation experiments; measures memorization, perturbation hallucinations and natural hallucinations under artificial corpus noise rather than random-label fitting and held-out accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: Hallucination outcomes vary with memorization metric, corpus-noise pattern, translation direction and downstream data-generation process.

fits_no_version.finding: The highest-memorization samples produce more perturbation hallucinations than random samples under chrF, BLEU and exact-match memorization estimates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this NMT setting, estimated sample memorization is associated with susceptibility to source-perturbation hallucinations.

fits_no_version.finding: Memorized samples have lower attention entropy and greater average attention to the final source token.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorized and randomly selected NMT samples differ in their decoder cross-attention statistics.

fits_no_version.finding: Held-out BLEU remains similar across noise conditions, with modest decreases for UR in both translation directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These NMT models largely retain in-domain translation performance despite added invalid sentence pairs.

fits_no_version.finding: All KD outputs have higher estimated hallucination counts than the original parallel corpus; UR has the largest count. BT counts vary substantially across noise patterns, without a clean-model BT comparator.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Estimated hallucinations in generated translation data depend on training noise and the data-generation process.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Most experiments use IWSLT 2014 due to computational cost. Hallucination detection for natural hallucinations is approximate; the authors state it misses many oscillatory hallucinations. The attention comparison is aggregated over sets, and uncertainty estimates are not stated.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fixed-random-label fitting and the corresponding natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed to fit.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization and tuning-dependent differences.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout interventions; dropout is held at 0.3.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps and comparisons with alternative measures.
Removing highly memorized versus equally many random examples, retraining and comparing held-out accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: No listed version receives a verdict. Adapting an original source's estimator is not itself a test or operational use of its memorized-example removal finding. Additional hallucination results in Figure 3 and Tables 5–6 fall outside all eight versions, so they do not require missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
No network-width sweep or test-error comparison beyond the width needed to fit.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer comparison.
Dropout is held at 0.3 in the reported model setups; no dropout comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison of generalization gaps.
No removal and retraining comparison for memorized examples and test accuracy.

rows.operation_detail: Estimate natural hallucinations in sequence-level knowledge-distillation outputs generated by the no-noise model.
rows.note: The authors describe increases for all noisy models relative to the initial parallel corpus; KD-None is the no-noise comparator.
rows.check: Correct estimated hallucination counts; these measure generated KD data rather than a listed generalization effect.

rows.check: The value 12 is correct. The note repeats an author statement contradicted by the tables: RU has fewer estimated hallucinations than RR in BT, and UU has fewer than RR in KD.
